description: We are Tronador, a group of students from Rosario, Argentina. We are interested in engineering, physics, programming, economics and, of course, space!
summary: Arcadia is a simulator that immerses users in an authentic mission on Mars—specifically, in an area known as Arcadia Planitia. The simulator is developed using actual data from past NASA missions, along with precise calculations required for the operation of our first space base. The mission’s objective is to expand the habitable surface area to accommodate more guests and, ultimately, to establish a habitat on Mars.
details:
ARCADIA is a simulator that immerses anyone in a realistic mission on Mars, specifically in a region called Arcadia Planitia (≈40° N). The simulator is built on and supported by real NASA data from previous missions, together with engineering calculations for the operation of our first space base. The goal of the mission is to expand the habitable surface so the outpost can keep receiving new crew members and, progressively, establish a permanent habitat on Mars. The game offers two levels of experience and difficulty — Junior Mission and Commander Mission — so that both young learners and adults experience first-hand the trade-offs between life support, radiation shielding, power and food production that decide whether a mission succeeds or fails.

The outpost is designed for a crew of 3 astronauts. All initial materials are brought from Earth; everything else is produced in situ from local resources: oxygen, methane (also used to produce plastics), water extracted from the ground, and food grown in the habitat's farm. The design also accounts for the daily exercise the crew must perform to avoid bone and muscle loss caused by Mars's reduced gravity (0.38 g).

2. System Architecture: How Everything Is Connected

The outpost works as a closed network of energy and matter flows. The three diagrams prepared by the team describe it in three layers: (a) the power matrix, (b) the gas and water cycle, and (c) the general interconnection tree that combines both and adds the downstream uses of methane.

2.1 Power matrix (sources → distribution node → loads)

Three independent energy sources feed a single electrical distribution node (power bus):

  • Kilopower nuclear reactors (KRUSTY — Kilopower Reactor Using Stirling Technology): the base-load source, operating 24 hours a day regardless of sunlight or dust storms. Besides electricity, they deliver waste heat (thermal energy) used to melt ice and to heat the aquaponic fish tanks.
  • External solar field (photovoltaic panels): 10 modules that supply daytime power.
  • Reversible solid-oxide fuel cell (r-SOFC): the chemical energy storage and emergency backup. It converts stored methane + oxygen back into electricity when needed, and can run in reverse to store surplus energy.

The distribution node then feeds every consumer of the outpost: the habitat (life support ECLSS), the aquaponic farm (BLSS), avionics/communications/EVA, the MOXIE oxygen reactor, the water electrolyzer, ice extraction, the methanation (Sabatier) reactor and the polyethylene (plastics) plant. Thermal energy from the reactors is routed separately to ice melting and to heating the tilapia ponds.

2.2 Gas and water cycle

  1. Water extraction: subsurface ice (10–20 cm deep in Arcadia Planitia) is extracted, melted with reactor heat, and stored as liquid water.
  2. Water use: part of the water goes directly to the habitat for human consumption and the farm; the rest goes to the PEM electrolyzer, which splits it into oxygen (O₂) and hydrogen (H₂).
  3. Breathing loop: the crew exhales carbon dioxide (CO₂), which is captured in the cabin and sent to the scaled-up MOXIE reactor (15×). MOXIE splits CO₂ into breathable oxygen (sent to the habitat's O₂ reserve) and carbon monoxide (CO).
  4. Methane synthesis: CO from MOXIE and H₂ from the electrolyzer feed the methanation (Sabatier) reactor: CO + 3H₂ → CH₄ + H₂O. The by-product water returns to the water loop.
  5. Nitrogen: a small amount of nitrogen, separated when compressing Martian air, is supplied to the habitat as a buffer gas to make up for leaks and airlock losses.

2.3 Downstream uses of methane (CH₄)

The methane produced is distributed to four destinations:

  • F1 · Plastics plant (HDPE): Stage A, oxidative coupling of methane (OCM) → ethylene (C₂H₄); Stage B, purification with zeolites; Stage C, polymerization → high-density polyethylene (HDPE). The HDPE is turned into 3D-printing filament by a micro-extruder, and used both for radiation shielding and for spare parts printed on site.
  • F2 · Vehicles and propulsion: methalox propellant (liquid CH₄ / liquid O₂) for the Mars Ascent Vehicle (MAV), and fuel for heavy rovers and surface machinery.
  • F3 · Energy backup: the r-SOFC stores energy chemically; the reserve provides 1,375 kWh, i.e. 30 days of survival-mode autonomy.
  • F4 · Metallurgical reduction: a direct-reduction (DRI) furnace at 900 °C reduces Martian iron oxide with methane (Fe₂O₃ + CH₄) to produce sponge iron / steel as structural raw material.

3. Habitat Structure and Materials

General concept. The habitat modules are built from a titanium–aluminium alloy, chosen for its strength-to-weight ratio, which allows large amounts of construction material to be carried in a first launch. The whole structure is covered with a protective layer — high-density polyethylene plus Martian regolith — to shield the crew from radiation. Internally, the modules include a rubber layer to absorb the different stresses produced by pressure differences.

The structural pre-design below covers cylindrical and hemispherical modules with an inner radius of 3 m, sized with thin-wall shell theory.

Per hemisphere, the regolith volume is 119.1 m³ (178.6 t) and the HDPE volume 8.9 m³ (8.5 t). Total reduction versus the reference: from 308 t to 187 t per hemisphere (−39 %). HDPE creep under compression is negligible; its thermal expansion (15 mm per metre of panel for ΔT = 100 K) is not, and requires joints between panels. The HDPE is the same material produced on site by the plastics plant (F1), which closes the loop between the methane chain and radiation protection.

Not yet verified: the cosmic-ray shielding equivalence of HDPE + regolith (209 g/cm²) versus 2 m of regolith (300 g/cm²). HDPE is assumed to be more effective per unit mass (hydrogen-rich), but this must be confirmed with a radiation transport code (GEANT4 or OLTARIS) against an annual target dose.

4. Gas System: Demand, Equipment and External Storage

4.1 Daily requirements and production (3 astronauts in Arcadia Planitia)

  • Metabolic oxygen consumption: 3.36 kg/day (breathing including 2 hours of daily exercise).
  • Carbon dioxide exhaled: 3.30 kg/day (captured in the cabin and sent directly to processing).
  • Subsurface ice extraction required: 25.38 kg/day (25.4 L/day net: 2.70 kg for life support and 22.68 kg to produce fuel with surplus energy).
  • Surplus oxygen: 41.76 kg/day (after covering 100 % of crew breathing).
  • Methane: 11.28 kg/day (for heavy rovers, energy storage, the return rocket and electrical backup).
  • Make-up nitrogen: 0.15–0.30 kg/day (extracted as a by-product of compressing Martian air, to compensate for leaks and airlocks).

5.2 Generators and backup

  • Kilopower KRUSTY reactors (2 units): each unit is ~3.0 m tall with a 4.2 m diameter umbrella-type radiator on top, weighs ~1,650 kg (including radiation shielding), and is installed inside a crater or behind a regolith berm 100–150 m away from the habitat.
  • Emergency generator (reversible solid-oxide fuel cell, r-SOFC): occupies 0.18 m³ (180 L) and weighs 140 kg. It converts the reserve methane and oxygen into electricity. With the 180 kg methane reserve it delivers 1,375 kWh, sustaining the habitat in survival mode (1.9 kWe) for 30 full days without solar or nuclear power.

6. External Solar Panels: Characteristics and Layout

To reach 140 m² of active area in Arcadia Planitia (40° N latitude, where peak noon irradiance is ~380 W/m²), the external photovoltaic field is divided into 10 independent modules:

  • Architecture and quantity: 10 deployable modules of 14.0 m² each (arranged in 5 pairs or external rows).
  • Dimensions per module: 7.0 m long × 2.0 m wide (2 mm deployed thickness on a lightweight carbon-fibre tubular frame).
  • Mass: 26 kg per module (1.85 kg/m²), 260 kg in total for the whole solar field.
  • Output per module: 1.20 kWe (1,200 W) at noon peak and 10.8 kWh generated per day.

Installation rules to optimize production:

  1. Fixed latitudinal tilt toward the south: since the base lies in the Martian northern hemisphere, panels are tilted toward the equator (south).
  2. Single-axis (east–west) solar tracking: each module has a low-power motorized actuator (< 5 W) that rotates the panel from east to west following the daily solar arc, increasing daily energy output by 28 % compared to a fixed horizontal panel.
  3. Electrodynamic dust shield (EDS): a transparent coating on the front face that applies high-voltage electrical pulses every sol at sunset to remove deposited dust.
  4. Physical spacing between modules: rows must be installed at least 12–15 m apart so that the shadow of one row does not fall on the next.

7. Food Production

7.1 Hybrid protein system: tilapia + microalgae

Nile or red tilapia is the base fish, combined with photobioreactors of omega-3-rich microalgae (e.g. Nannochloropsis, Schizochytrium, Chlorella vulgaris). Advantages:

  • A robust fish that is easy to raise and breed in microgravity or partial gravity (0.38 g on Mars).
  • Microalgae serve as a direct food source or as a base for DHA/EPA-rich feed pellets, and as an additional biofilter that fixes CO₂ and releases O₂.
  • Fish meat with a fatty-acid profile comparable to marine fish can be achieved if 5–10 % of the diet consists of omega-3 microalgae.

The fish tanks are heated with waste heat from the Kilopower reactors, and the ammonium excreted by the fish provides nitrogen to the crops (aquaponics).

7.2 Vegetables

Each astronaut must eat 1 kg of vegetables per day. Selected crops:

  • Lettuce (main vegetable): fast growth, low nutrient demand per kg of food produced, tolerates repeated leaf cutting; provides fibre and vitamins A, C and K.
  • Microgreens (broccoli, peas, etc.): very high nutritional value per weight, omega fatty acids, and provide a lot of nitrogen when composted.
  • Spinach: iron, calcium and potassium.
  • Peas: grow in vertical space, diversify the diet and provide plenty of protein.
  • Potato: a resilient crop with a high contribution of iron and carbohydrates, plus some calcium, zinc and vitamin C.

8. Limitations

The structural design is a thin-wall pre-design and is not certifiable. Still missing: finite-element analysis, soil–structure interaction and asymmetric regolith loads, S-N curves for welds, radiation dose with transport simulation, and site geotechnical data. The 50 m/s design wind, the 2.0 safety factor, the 10 daily airlock cycles, the weld misalignment and the K_IC value are assumptions.
